tagline.text: A twin waterfall about 26 m high, hidden in the hills of Ilocos Sur

location.label: Location
location.text: Barangay Baballasioan, end of Pinsal Falls Road, Santa Maria, Ilocos Sur

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: June–November, mid to late rainy season (high water flow); November–May dry season (easier access)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300~1,000 (per person, day trip, excluding transport from Manila)

children.text: Pinsal Falls lies at the eastern edge of Santa Maria in Ilocos Sur, close to the border with Abra. A stream about 85 feet (about 26 m) high splits in two as it drops, which is why it is called the Twin Falls, and in 2019 it was declared a tourist destination by law. It makes a good day trip from Vigan.
Pinsal Falls sits at the far inland end of the municipality of Santa Maria in Ilocos Sur, in the mountain area of Baballasioan next to Abra province. It is reached by about
of paved road from Santa Maria town proper, and because far fewer people come here than to famous cities such as Vigan or Laoag, it is a quiet place to enjoy nature.

Several travel guides give the height of the main falls as about 85 feet (about 26 m). The water splits into two streams partway down the rock cliff, so locals also call it the Twin Falls. The water gathers in an emerald pool, and further up, small natural pools are said to step up one above another. The largest of them is called Tugot ni Angalo, which local legend says is the footprint of a giant.

The falls were declared a tourist destination on August 22, 2019 by Republic Act No. 11409, which directs the Department of Tourism (DOT) to prioritize their development. The area defined by the law is about 75 hectares. The site is still not well equipped, though, and many visitors report a lack of facilities such as toilets, showers and restaurants. Go expecting a natural setting rather than amenities.

Santa Maria, close to Vigan, is also home to Santa Maria Church, one of the UNESCO World Heritage Baroque churches, so combining the church and the falls in a single day is widely recommended. What follows is based on facts confirmed from several travel reports dated 2015 to 2026 and from the official law. Fees and facilities change often, so please verify them locally.

blocks.title: A twin waterfall about 26 m high

children.text: The stream splitting in two partway down the cliff is the main sight here. Several guides give the main falls a height of about 85 feet, and when the water is high the spray reaches well in front of the falls.
On the pool in front of the falls, local residents take visitors on a bamboo raft close to the foot of the falls. Reported prices vary, from about
per person to group rates, so ask for the exact amount before you board.

There is a viewpoint on the opposite side from which you can look over the whole falls, and climbing the upper stairs and rocky path gives a wider view of the two-tiered falls and the emerald natural pools. The stairs are narrow and rusty in places, so take care.

The pool below the falls is clear and cold. The current can be fast on days when the water is up or right after rain, so follow the local caretakers' advice and swim only when it is safe. Some reports say life vests can be rented.
Along the trail below there are cottages where you can rest, reported at about
depending on the visit. Bring a packed lunch and drinks and relax in the shade to the sound of the falls.

blocks.title: A combined trip with Santa Maria Church

children.text: Santa Maria Church in town is an 18th-century Baroque church at the top of a long stone staircase on a hill. Stopping by on the way to the falls lets you see both nature and history in one day.

If you go early in the morning there are hardly any people, the air is cool for walking, and the light is good for photos. Some visitors have arrived in town around dawn and reached the falls in the early morning.

items.title: Day trip from Vigan
items.subtitle: Falls and church in one day

children.text: From Vigan, take a southbound bus (Partas, Philippine Rabbit and others heading toward Laoag or Abra) to Santa Maria. Many reports say it takes about
under 1 hour
from Vigan, and you can get off in front of Savemore or in the town center.
Hire a tricycle in town to the end of Pinsal Falls Road. The distance is about
, so it takes
20–45 minutes
one way, and it helps to arrange in advance for the driver to take you back.
Leave your bag at the reception area and follow the trail to the viewpoint. After seeing the whole falls, take a raft to the foot of the falls.
If it looks safe, swim in the pool, then rest in a cottage and eat the lunch you brought.
Return to town by tricycle and have lunch. In town there is a fast-food outlet next to the Savemore Market and an Ilocano eatery.
Climb the stone steps of Santa Maria Church and look around the church and bell tower. Afterward, go on by bus to Vigan or your next destination.
All times are examples. They vary with bus schedules and tricycle bargaining, so leave some slack.

items.title: Overnight bus from Manila
items.subtitle: Arrive at dawn, head home in the afternoon

children.text: Take an overnight bus from Pasay or Cubao in Manila bound for Vigan, Bangued or Laoag.
Arrive in Santa Maria. There may be no tricycles before daylight, so wait near the terminal or pass the time over breakfast.
Take the first tricycle to the falls and see them in the early hours when few people are around.
Return to town, visit Santa Maria Church and have a combined breakfast and lunch.
Go on to Vigan to see Calle Crisologo, or take a bus back to Manila.
Overnight buses vary in arrival time, so allow some slack. Reports say there is no lodging around the falls and overnight stays are not allowed, so staying in Vigan is the realistic option.

Buses to Ilocos, including Partas, Philippine Rabbit, Viron and Dominion, leave from the Cubao, Pasay and Sampaloc terminals in Manila. Buses bound for Vigan, Bangued (Abra) and Laoag pass through Santa Maria.
Travel time varies widely between reports, at about
6–10 hours
. Fares depend on the bus class (regular, deluxe, super express), and one report put the one-way fare at about
(2018). Check the current fare with the bus company.
Tell the driver in advance to let you off in Santa Maria town or in front of Savemore.
Bus schedules and fares change often. Check the bus company's announcements before you leave.

items.title: By car or van from Manila

children.text: Head north via NLEX, SCTEX and TPLEX toward La Union and Ilocos Sur. Searching for "Pinsal Falls" in Google Maps will give you directions.

Some reports say the junction is confusing where you take the Santa Maria–Burgos road from Santa Maria Church and turn right onto Pinsal Falls Road, so keep following the "Pinsal Falls Road" signs to the end.
Reports say there is parking at the entrance to the falls, with a small parking fee.
The nearest commercial airport is Laoag International Airport (LAO). Check the airlines' announcements to see whether domestic flights between Manila and Laoag operate and at what times.
From Laoag to Santa Maria you travel by bus or van, passing through Vigan on the way. Travel time varies greatly with traffic.
Air routes change with the season, so check the latest information before booking.
A tricycle from Santa Maria town is the most common way. Reports vary, at about
one way and about
round trip, so negotiate the round-trip fare and waiting time before you ride.
The distance is about
and the trip is described as taking
20–45 minutes
. Reports say the road is paved all the way to the falls.
There is also a record of reaching the falls on foot from the Pilar side in Abra province, but this needs local confirmation.
The road has no streetlights, so avoid plans that bring you back after dark.

The falls look very different depending on the water flow. In the rainy season the flow is abundant and impressive, but paths are slippery and the current can be strong; in the dry season the paths are easy to walk and the water is clear, but the flow can shrink.
Ilocos Sur has a fairly distinct dry season (generally
November–May
) and rainy season (generally
June–October
). Recommended seasons differ between reports, so check recent local conditions before you go.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Many reports say the water color is good and the paths are fairly dry, so walking is easy.
Some reports say the flow drops sharply and thins out, so check conditions before you visit.
The flow is at its richest, but paths are slippery and access may be restricted during typhoons or heavy rain.

items.label: Entrance fee
items.note: The 2026 guide says free; some reports mention a ₱20 environmental fee

items.label: Bus from Manila
items.note: ₱670 in a 2018 report; varies by class

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
There is no lodging around the falls, and reports say the caretakers do not allow camping or overnight stays. The nearest accommodation is in Vigan, about
30–55 minutes
away by bus according to many reports. Hotels such as Hotel Veneto de Vigan and Hotel Luna often come up in reports.

Many reports say there are no restaurants or stores around the falls, so bring water, snacks and a packed lunch. In Santa Maria town, a fast-food outlet next to Savemore Market and Ilocano eateries such as Gacusana's Food House are mentioned. Local Ilocos foods such as longganisa (sausage) and Abra-style pancit loglog are also worth trying.
Go early in the morning. There are fewer people, it is cooler, and photos come out well.
Bring plenty of cash, mostly small bills. There are no ATMs nearby, and the raft, cottage and tricycle fees are paid in cash.
Bring water, snacks, a trash bag, a change of clothes and a towel. There is no changing room, so it is best to wear your swimwear underneath.
The rocky paths are wet and slippery, so water shoes or shoes with good grip are best; avoid flip-flops.
Agree on the round-trip fare and waiting time with the tricycle driver first. It may not be easy to find a ride back.
Get off the bus in front of Savemore or in the town center, and check the last bus time back to Manila in advance.
Follow the local caretakers' advice for swimming, and it is safer to rent and wear a life vest.
Take all your trash back with you. Reports say there is no garbage collection.

During the rainy season and typhoon season the water can rise suddenly and dangerously, and access may be restricted. Check conditions with the Santa Maria town hall or local caretakers before you leave.
The stairs to the upper viewpoint are narrow and rusty in places, and some sections have no handrails. Be especially careful with children and older visitors.
Some reports say the caretakers forbid climbing to the top of the falls. Follow their instructions.
The road has no streetlights, so travel after dark is dangerous. Return to town before sunset.
Many reports say there are no toilets or showers, or too few. Prepare ahead and take care of this in town.
Fees, operating arrangements and access rules change often, so check the latest announcements locally.

An 18th-century Baroque church on a hill in Santa Maria town, listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The long stone staircase and the freestanding bell tower are striking, and it is a good stop on the way back from the falls by tricycle.
A UNESCO World Heritage city whose Spanish colonial streets are well preserved. It is about
under 1 hour
away by bus, so it works well as a base for lodging, meals and transport.
The main city of Ilocos Norte, home to Laoag International Airport. It is a handy base when you combine this trip with a northern Ilocos itinerary.
A UNESCO World Heritage Baroque church in Ilocos Norte, known for its massive buttresses. It fits well into a loop around Ilocos.
